The Primary Process: A Reconceptualization

Stanley Palombo MD

Stanley Palombo

35 Wisconsin Circle
Chevy Chase, Md. 20815

Stanley Palombo  

Freud formed his theory of the primary process (1900, 1911), the heart of his “metapsychology,” in the conceptual mold of nineteenth-century physics. Despite its historical importance at the birth of psychoanalysis, it remains biologically anachronistic, internally inconsistent, and unable to account for Freud's clinical observations showing that primary process phenomena convey information as well as motivational force. Despite these serious signs of obsolescence, Freud's theory of primary process activity has not been a major topic for scientific discussion in many years.

Since Freud's death in 1939, classical physics has been replaced as the conceptual ideal for biology and psychology by a new theoretical framework drawn from the information sciences. In the life sciences today, generalization and simplification are no longer the primary aims of the investigator. Scientific models constructed within the new framework are designed to capture the richness, complexity, and individuality of biological and psychological phenomena. These models allow practical solutions to problems involving the interaction and mutual regulation of complex systems, from the level of the genetic code to the level of linguistic and problem-solving performance in humans.

Dr. Palombo is Clinical Associate Professor, Department of Psychiatry, George Washington University.

Bearer of the Secret

Louis Micheels MD

Louis Micheels

129 Kings Highway North
Westport, Connecticut 06880

Louis Micheels  

“Let it be said to you, the most dangerous thing in the camp is to know anything.” That is what the “old-timers” say, and they have experience.

—H. Langbein, Die Stärkeren (translated by Micheels)

Understanding the holocaust, its impact and its lessons may sound like a reasonable, albeit difficult task, but has unexpected obstacles. These obstacles have formed a formidable wall that has stood in the way of grasping the essence of this catastrophic event. They consist of psychological barriers to knowing, remembering, and communicating what has happened.

Although after his ascent to power Hitler flaunted his plans for extermination of the Jews, and the press initially spelled out his pronouncements in detail, the general unwillingness of Jews and non-Jews alike to accept the fact that Hitler meant what he said played into the Nazis' diabolical attempt to keep the Final Solution secret. To this end they selected sites that suited their purpose of isolating the extermination camps from the rest of the world. Auschwitz was chosen primarily with the requirement of secrecy in mind. It was located in a sparsely populated, rural, and swampy area in Upper Silesia, now southwestern Poland. It seemed to be out of the reach of Allied airplanes and, therefore, safe from aerial reconnaissance.

Dr. Micheels is Associate Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Yale University School of Medicine.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

Donald Silver Issue Editor

Donald Silver

Donald Silver  

Gedo's review of Lichtenberg's clinical vignettes is a fitting close to the commentaries in this issue, because it reminds us once more that Lichtenberg is first and foremost a clinician, and his immersion in the experimental and observational literature of infant research was undertaken with respect to clinical goals. It is to his great credit that, in the course of this undertaking, he has initiated an exchange among developmentalists, theoreticians, and clinicians of various persuasions. By taking a pioneering first step in showing how new insights into early development bear on psychoanalytic practice, he has provided new and compelling evidence in support of the timeworn psychoanalytic belief that assumptions about development and issues of therapy go hand in hand, being, in the end, two sides of the coin. That his theory of therapy should be critically probed by a theoretician of the stature of Friedman will probably bother him no more than the fact that his technical recommendations should be wrestled with by a clinician of the stature of Gedo. But then I suspect he would be equally pleased that his cautious developmental constructions have been subject to amplification by researchers such as Gaensbauer, Stechler, and Dowling, energetically contested by Demos, and contrasted with separation-individuation theory by Bergman and Pollens. In the end, he should be content with Basch's verdict, seconded by Friedman and Gedo, that he has indeed put his finger on the big questions confronting psychoanalysis and infant research, inviting a dialogue from which all are bound to profit.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Prologue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor and Donald Silver Issue Editors

Donald Silver

Donald Silver  

This issue explores the widespread uses in psychoanalysis of references to the mirror. Researchers use observations of infants in front of mirrors to draw conclusions about development. Lacan made a hypothesis based on his rendering of one such observation a pivotal part of his theory. As a metaphor, mirroring is mentioned in almost every account of mother-infant interaction. Kohut described mirror transferences as a principal finding in all psychoanalyses. Other theoreticians, such as Mahler and Winnicott, weave the concept of mirroring into their formulations, each giving it a different degree of significance. Sartre developed an epistemological position using mirror experience as a foundation. Clinicians have referred to mirror dreams and to the mirror in fantasies and memories. In studies of applied analysis, the mirror as it appears in painting and in literature has been a fertile stimulus for speculation about its deeper symbolic meaning.

It is interesting to note that this widespread fascination with the mirror has not always been with us. The total body of Freud's work reveals only a few uses of this rich source for metaphor: the mirror the analyst holds before the analysand, reflecting back to him only that which the analysand provides, adding no values or direction of his own (Freud, 1912); the association between the mirror, the double, and the sense of the uncanny (1919); and the mirror as part of a child's game of disappearing (1920). These historical beginnings of the mirror, actual and as metaphor, can easily be related to what has evolved since, but do not in themselves foretell of the depth of understanding plumbed, using the mirror as a point of reference. To explore these developments — many quite recent in origin — we have planned this issue around contributors who use the mirroring interaction of mother and infant as a point of departure for a discussion of the mirror and of mirroring.

[[RunningHead]]

Rearview-Mirror Dreams

Leon Berman MD

Leon Berman

280 N. Woodward, Suite 304
Birmingham, Michigan 48011

Leon Berman  

The psychoanalytic literature contains a few reports of mirror dreams but no references, to my knowledge, of rearview-mirror dreams. In this paper I consider a group of manifest dreams containing rearview mirrors along with some rearview mirror associations. These data suggest that certain meanings are frequently represented and expressed through the use of the rearview mirror, and that these meanings differ from those usually attributed to the face-on or vis-à-vis mirror dream. One must be careful about attributing too specific a meaning to any dream element, especially with limited data and, therefore, the hypotheses presented herein must be considered tentative. I hope they will stimulate further discussion and the sharing of clinical data.

A review of the literature on mirror dreams shows general agreement as to their narcissistic implications: to preserve narcissistic integrity and to defend against fears of object loss. Elkisch (1957) described mirroring phenomena in psychotic and borderline patients attempting to retrieve their lost sense of self. Miller (1948) believed mirror dreams occur in narcissistic patients and reflect the ego's struggle to acknowledge an unconscious conflict being mobilized in the analysis. Eisnitz (1961) considered the mirror dream an attempt to defend against narcissistic mortification, the threatening part of the superego having been split off and projected to the mirror. Kohut (1971)

Dr. Berman is a Lecturer at the Michigan Psychoanalytic Institute and Assistant Professor of Psychiatry, Wayne State University College of Medicine.

Epilogue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor and Donald Silver Issue Editor

Donald Silver

Donald Silver  

All the contributors to this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry, we believe, take the mirroring interaction of mother and infant as a point of departure — whether explicitly or implicitly — even as they explore different vicissitudes attendant to the outcome of this first and prototypical mirroring relationship. We have examinations of both the intrapsychic and interactional nature of successful mother-infant mirroring, along with examinations of the developmental and clinical outcomes of mother-infant mirroring that has been derailed. We also have a range of commentaries — clinical, philosophical, art-historical — on the varieties of self-knowledge and self-expression that embody different sequelae to the infant's earliest mirroring experiences. In short, we have a rich cross section of views on the various tributaries that feed into the individual's sense of self, as mediated by and through the mirroring experiences of life.

[[RunningHead]]

The Elusive Infant

E. Demos Ed.D.

E. Demos

27 Winsor Avenue
Watertown, MA 02172

E. Demos  

Over the last two decades a vast increase in research findings about infants has yielded an astonishing amount of new information. It is not an exaggeration to say that we are currently witnessing a revolution in our thinking about the infant's capabilities and the developmental process. And, as in all revolutions, older established theories are likely to be radically altered or discarded. In this particular revolution, the two theories most vulnerable to challenges are the developmental theories proposed by psychoanalysis and by Piaget. Psychoanalysts have become increasingly interested in the findings from infant research and are asking whether and in what ways their clinical work and theoretical assumptions must be affected. Joseph Lichtenberg's book Psychoanalysis and Infant Research is just such an inquiry.

Lichtenberg is very clear that the data of psychoanalysis deals with symbolic representations of experience—verbalizations of sensations, fantasies, memories—and that much of infant research deals with prerepresentational experiences—events that occur before the advent of language and the capacity for symbolic representations (roughly before 18 months of age). He nevertheless argues that the important question is whether the data from infant research “lend themselves to or indeed compel a reexamination of basic psychoanalytic hypotheses” (p. 4).

Dr. Demos is Assistant Professor in Child Psychiatry and Pediatrics, Boston University Medical School.

Psychoanalysis as Critique of Ideology

Barnaby Barratt PHD

Barnaby Barratt

144 Fairfax Drive
Birmingham, MI 48009

Barnaby Barratt  

No wonder the ancient cultures of conceit, in his technique of unsettlement foresaw the fall of princes, the collapse of their lucrative patterns of frustration:

if he succeeded, why, the Generalized Life would become impossible, the monolith of State be broken and prevented the cooperation of avengers.

— W. H. Auden (1939), In Memory of Sigmund Freud.

What is the political and sociocultural challenge of psychoanalytic discovery and psychoanaltyic praxis? And why indeed might Freud's psychology be considered the discourse of our unsettlement?

Psychoanalysis is at a critical juncture of its intellectual, practical, and organizational history. It is caught between, on the one side, its institutional domestication as a technology of adaptation with the concomitant occlusion of its original radicalism as a critique of the human condition, and, on the other side, the attempt to return to this radicalism in the redefinition of the scientific praxis of psychoanalysis as an emancipatory work aspiring to a vision of the human subject, its world, and its potentialities.

I would like to thank Dr. W. Randolph Earnest of the University of Michigan for the many informal discussions we have shared on the topic of ideology. The permission of Professor Edward Mendelson, and of Random House, Inc., to quote from the works of W. H. Auden, is gratefully acknowledged.

On the Dawn of Experience: The Past Recaptured

John Gedo MD

John Gedo

400 E. Randolph Street
Apt. 3724
Chicago, IL 60601

John Gedo  

In the past decade, Joseph Lichtenberg has done more than anyone else in the psychoanalytic community to keep open lines of communication among the increasingly isolated segments of our discipline. This ecumenical activity has taken him from a respected role as a psychoanalytic scholar and teacher into ever more influential positions as the organizer of panels and symposia, the editor of Psychoanalytic Inquiry and a series of topical books, and now the author of an ambitious monograph of Psychoanalysis and Infant Research. There could be no more fitting way to acknowledge Lichtenberg's invaluable services to psychoanalysis than to devote an issue of the journal he has guided with such distinction since its inception to his most ambitious effort in the service of science. For, despite its relative brevity, Lichtenberg's book is an essential building block if we are to achieve a new consensus within psychoanalysis to succeed the centrifugal tendencies of the last generation.

The threatened fragmentation of our field into hositle factions heatedly defending ideological partis pris has always been a byproduct of the fact that the psychoanalytic method yields relatively scant evidence about personality development in the preverbal period of life.

Dr. Gedo is a Training and Supervising Analyst at the Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis.

The Study of Infants Engenders Systemic Thinking

Gerald Stechler PHD

Gerald Stechler

18 Whittier Road
Lexington, MA 02173

Gerald Stechler  

Given the enormous breadth of psychoanalysis, it is inevitable that it finds itself in dialectical tension with other disciplines which also seek to answer the same fundamental questions about the nature of human existence. The encounters include fields as far-ranging as political science and neurophysiology. That psychoanalysis has been challenged by such diverse viewpoints is testimony to its comprehensiveness and explanatory force.

One of the more recent dialogues has been with a somewhat loosely knit field called infant research. The manner in which one proceeds with that dialogue and how it is resolved may be a function of how the questions are framed. For example, at psychoanalytic meetings the question may be formulated something like this:

“Psychoanalysis and infant research stem from two totally different data bases, the couch and the crib; they deal with two distinctly different realities, the subjective and the objective; they relate to two different time frames, the long-term retrospective and the short-term contemporaneous, and they have two different aims, therapeutic and scientific.

Dr. Stechler is Professor of Psychiatry, Boston University School of Medicine; Director of Child and Adolescent Services, Charles River Hospital; Faculty Member, Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute.

[[RunningHead]]

The Relevance of Infant Research for Psychoanalysis

Theodore Gaensbauer MD

Theodore Gaensbauer

3955 E. Exposition, #402D
Denver, CO 80209

Theodore Gaensbauer  

In psychoanalysis and infant research, Dr. Joseph Lichtenberg has taken on a challenging and important task, and succeeded admirably. As an infant researcher and recent graduate of the Denver Psychoanalytic Institute, I have special sympathy for the task Lichtenberg has set for himself, namely, to reconcile the differing points of view of the researcher and the clinician. Psychoanalysis and Infant Research presents a strong argument for the relevance of infant research for psychoanalytic theory and the need for clinical theory to take the newer findings into account. Clinicians reading this book will find an excellent review of infancy research data relevant to clinical and theoretical issues. Lichtenberg's summaries of the studies that have been done, and the implications he draws from them, are soundly based and consistent with the assumptions drawn by direct workers in the field. The degree of sophisticated understanding of infant research reflected in Lichtenberg's exposition is rare on the part of the clinician, and it is this combination which makes the book so valuable.

Because I am in such substantial agreement with Lichtenberg's ideas, I would like in this review to highlight a number of points he has made that I feel are of special importance and to expand on a few areas based on my own work in affect development in infancy.

Dr. Gaensbauer is an Associate Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, University of Colorado Health Sciences Center.

Mirror in Dreams: Symbol of Mother's Face

Donald Silver MD

Donald Silver

26502 Fourteen Mile Road
Franklin, Michigan 48025

Donald Silver  

The mirror as Metaphor is ubiquitous in language, art, history, myth, and dream. What can depth psychology and, more specifically the psychoanalytic theory of development, contribute to an understanding of the timeless mirror symbolism that permeates all these realms of human expression? We begin with the observation of infant researchers that, even moments after birth, the newborn seeks out the mother's eyes and face as the initial source of information and confirmation. When the newborn is presented with a variety of pictures, for example, it will invariably fix on the picture with a human face (Cohen & Salapatek, 1975; Brazelton, 1980; Lamb & Sherrod, 1981). When the caregiver is receptive to the infant's search gaze, orchestrating her voice, posture, and facial expression in response to the infant's exploratory visual gestures, a remarkable synchrony between the two results; researchers behold striking periods of in-tuneness between mother and infant, in which the latter contentedly gazes into the pool of tranquilizing reflection embodied in the former. The psychoanalytic theory of development imparts meaning to such observations by suggesting that the mother is the first “mirror” of the infant and, by implication, the first mirroring validator of the infant's dawning self-awareness.

Dr. Silver is an Assistant Professor of Psychiatry, Wayne State University College of Medicine, and a Lecturer at the Michigan Psychoanalytic Institute.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Prologue

Donald Silver Issue Editor

Donald Silver

Donald Silver  

The earliest acknowledgment of the potentially complementary relationship between psychoanalysis and infant research came from Freud himself. In his Three Essays (1905), he observed that

Psychoanalytic investigation, reaching back into childhood from a later time, and contemporary observation of children combine to indicate to us still other regularly active sources of sexual excitation. The direct observation of children has the disadvantage of working upon data which are easily misunderstandable; psycho-analysis is made difficult by the fact that it can only reach its data, as well as its conclusions, after long detours. But by co-operation the two methods can attain a satisfactory degree of certainty in their findings [p. 201].

In pointing to the need for cooperative exchange between these “two methods,” Freud testified to the fact that psychoanalysts and infant researchers define their tasks, and arrive at their goals, in very different ways. Psychoanalysts, focusing on the psychopathology of adults, attempt to reconstruct retrospectively the early circumstances bearing on the genesis of this psychopathology. Infant researchers, focusing on the normal infant, attempt to delineate patterns of behavior on the basis of direct observation. To thus highlight the fundamental orientation is, by implication, to allude to what each type of investigator is apt to overlook. The clinical analyst is frequently inattentive to what transpires during the first two years of life, when symbolic-representational mental functioning is subordinate to sensorimotor functioning in the sense of Piaget.

Some Clinical and Theoretical Implications of Infant Research

Michael Basch MD

Michael Basch

55 E. Washington Street
No. 3605
Chicago, IL 60602

Michael Basch  

Fifteen or so years ago, when I first became interested in what research based on direct infant observation and experiment might contribute to the practice and theory of psychoanalysis, it was still possible to read a relatively small number of publications and claim to have a reasonable grasp of what there was to be learned about this subject. No more. Both the quantity and sophistication of infant research have grown apace, and so, even if it offered nothing more than an excellent compendium and summary of what the psychoanalyst and dynamically oriented psychotherapist should know about the early development of tension regulation, Psychoanalysis and Infant Research would be one of the few volumes I would consider an absolute must for student, teacher, and practitioner, but Lichtenberg achieves much more than that.

I would recommend that the reader begin with Chapter 12. Entitled “The Psychoanalytic Situation and Infancy.” It is here that Lichtenberg summarizes the various ways in which analysts have tried to “reconstruct” the infant from the memories and associations of adults in analysis, and the adultomorphic misconceptions that arose in that process.

Dr. Basch is a Professor of Psychiatry, Rush Medical College in Chicago, and a Training and Supervising Analyst at the Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis.

Mirroring and Reflection: Some Philosophical Issues

Phyllis Morris PHD

Phyllis Morris

4 Proctor Avenue
Clinton, New York 13323

Phyllis Morris  

Ever since Descartes wrote about it in the 17th century, many Western philosophers have been interested in the nature of the human capacity to reflect. Although much of that interest has been motivated by a search for the epistemological foundations of science, some of it has been directed toward discovering the nature of the person who reflects (see Kierkegaard, 1849; Dennett, 1976; Taylor, 1976). The latter concern is central to the present paper. Most philosophers have taken a nondevelopmental approach, from the stance of the rational adult thinker, even when they are concerned about continuity of the person through time.

In the present paper I discuss two important philosophical theories of human reflection, those of Descartes and Hume. I am suggesting that although David Hume rejected some of Descartes's assumptions, he retained some important and very problematic Cartesian claims about the nature of mind, body, and reflection. These assumptions form the core of the dominant philosophical theory of reflection. I then sketch what I consider a more satisfactory account of reflection. Each of these theories may be seen as having possible implications for therapy.

Dr. Morris is Adjunct Associate Professor of Philosophy at Le Moyne College, Syracuse, New York.

Presented to the International Interdisciplinary Conference on Self and Identity, sponsored by the Welsh Branch of the British Psychological Society, Cardiff, July, 1984. I am grateful to J. M. Morris, R. T. Blackwood, and K. J. Morris for their comments on this paper.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Although freud's legacy assumes that every psychoanalytic proposition blends science and humanism, the authors of the papers in this issue devote special attention to the dignity, values and ideals of human life in the development of their thesis. Chessick advocates authenticity of choice; Lichtenberg stresses the experimental and regulatory effect of human relations; Palombo describes the approximation of conflicting life forces; Barratt raises questions about the alienation of self-consciousness; and Meissner addresses the need for theory to be broad enough to encompass the human condition. In the realm of science, only psychoanalysis has the methodology and conceptual power to deal with the causality and meaning of these issues.

Theodore Shapiro, editor of the Journal of the American Psychoanalytic Association, wrote “Editorial: Psychoanalysis, Philosophy and the Public” (1985). The editorial is a response to several recent reviews in the lay and intellectual press on Adolph Grünbaum's, The Foundation of Psychoanalysis (1984). The reviews question the validity of psychoanalysis as a science and its usefulness as a therapy. Shapiro challenged psychoanalysts to develop a strategy to respond to the criticism, particularly whether psychoanalysis has a valid vital foundation within the scientific realm. We believe that Shapiro has articulated a crucial requirement to which psychoanalysts must respond. The success of our efforts will depend on how well psychoanalysts can further develop the unique scientific and humanistic capacities of psychoanalysis. We believe the accounting of Freud's legacy the papers in this issue provide are a fundamental foundation for the task ahead.

Humanism and the Science of Psychoanalysis

Joseph Lichtenberg MD

Joseph Lichtenberg

1616 Eighteenth St., N. W.
Washington, DC 20009

Joseph Lichtenberg  

Psychoanalysis, in the view of its founders, was a new and much needed science of the human mind. As such it had a highly troubled relationship with the other sciences, whose leaders regarded its basic data, the case histories, as more “romances” or novels than hard, experimentally derived facts. And to further the relative isolation of its pioneers, many followers of the humanities regarded psychoanalytic theory as esoteric and its incursions into explications of literature and the arts as amateurish or debasing. Despite this opposition, Freud became recognized universally as a great thinker, and psychoanalysis became a powerful force in twentieth century life. Now, in the last two decades of the century—nearly a hundred years since the beginning of psychoanalysis—where does psychoanalysis stand with respect to its old companions and foes, the humanities and the sciences? More important, what can be said about the future?

In the opening section of this essay I indicate that in the beginning Freud took a stand that created an arbitrary dichotomy between psychoanalysis as science and as humanism by choosing religion as the representative of the latter. At the same time, Freud himself applied his science, that is, his discoveries, to a full array of the subjects that comprise the humanities.

Dr. Lichtenberg is on the faculty of the Washington Psychoanalytic Institute.

Dr. Lichtenberg has concocted an enlightening and sometimes daring brew, a potpourri of ingredients which begins with the eye-opening findings of the “new” infant research and, after a tour through a dozen topics, arrives at a wide-ranging discussion of analytic interpretation and cure. Reflections on the Psychological and Social Function of Remembering the Holocaust

Martin Bergmann

Martin Bergmann

1136 Fifth Avenue
New York, New York 10028

Martin Bergmann  

The holocaust is an event in world history and the history of our century. However, since Jews were the primary targets for Hitler's Final Solution and most survivors are Jews, the Holocaust is an event that took place within Jewish history. The traditional Jewish attitude toward trauma is therefore relevant to the way the Holocaust is remembered and commemorated. To what purpose should the Holocaust be remembered? For those whose lives were not directly touched by the Holocaust, the question can be reformulated: To what purpose should the Holocaust be brought into social awareness? It is relatively easy for a psychoanalyst studying the effect of the Holocaust on the second generation to discover the deleterious effects of denying, isolating, or repressing what children of survivors know about the Holocaust. We psychoanalysts usually take for granted that it is better to remember. The individual may wish to unburden himself by trying to forget, but the community, in this case the Jewish community, always exerts pressure in the direction of remembering.

Dr. Bergmann is Co-Chairman of the study group examining The Effect of the Holocaust on the Second Generation. The group was sponsored by the New York Psychoanalytic Institute and was a recipient of a research grant from the American Psychoanalytic Association.

In this communication I raised some disturbing questions. I am grateful to a number of friends who helped me clarify these issues. They include Ruth and Peter Gay, Paulina and Otto Kernberg, Yosef Yerushalmi, Janine Chasseguet-Smirgel, John Gedo, and Maria Bergmann. Needless to say, I alone am responsible for the thoughts presented.

The Frantic Retreat From the Mind to the Brain: American Psychiatry in Mauvaise Foi

Richard Chessick M.D. Ph.D.

Richard Chessick

Suite 628
636 Church Street
Evanston, IL 60201

Richard Chessick  

Summary: Mental Health of the Psychiatrist

I have tried to demonstrate that American psychiatry is retreating to self-confinement within a biological paradigm that manifests Sartre's notion of bad faith. I have presented five alternative paradigms: those of Freudian psychoanalysis, Husserl's phenomenology, Sartre's existentialism, Lacanian psychoanalysis, and Kohut's psychology of the self, which are authentic in that they deal directly with the basic choices and issues that every human being in society has to contend with and they recognize fully in their various ways the etiologic importance of personal and collective psychic mythology and psychic realities.

I have reviewed the dangers of self-pronounced “eclecticism” and have warned how this attempt to avoid facing the issues and to hide behind an inauthentic and confused orientation may be responded to by society with a massive antipsychiatry movement and a spate of malpractice suits. Abroms (1983) recognizes that “Eclecticism has too much the connotation of superficiality, of ‘jack-of-all-trades, master of none,’ to capture the stringent requirements of modern psychiatric professionalism” (p. 744), and he takes a constructive step forward in suggesting his conception of “serial pluralism.” We need more ideas like this.

398

I have pointed out the dangers in residency training of whiplashing the resident back and forth between alternating alliances, and I wish to pull this discussion together by a final focus on the mental health of both the resident and the psychiatrist and their families. It is clear that the ordinary stress of being a resident in psychiatry is greatly increased if the resident is shuttled back and forth and presented with a confused orientation in his training. There is no objection to presenting the resident with several clearly different paradigms, but it is dangerous to attempt to combine them all under the rubric of eclecticism, which contains no psychiatric identity at all.

Probably of the most interest is the effect on the psychiatrist and his or her loved ones of a professional practice that devotes itself to avoiding authentic issues, the psychiatrist pretending to be something like a specialist in internal medicine who deals with mental disorders. Is there a connection between living in this chronically disavowed state and the allegedly high incidence of alcoholism, drug taking, and suicide among psychiatrists and in the medical profession generally? Those living in this chronically disavowed state harbor a secret cynicism and despair that is sometimes first reflected in emotional disturbances in the spouse or the children of the psychiatrist. It seems logical to me that, as the psychiatrist ages, the boredom and existential malaise engendered by an inauthentic practice of “eclectic” psychiatry or, even worse, of biological reductionism in psychiatry, will lead to an increasingly dysfunctional and despairing state.

In my experience (Chessick, 1977c), from the treatment of psychiatrists and their families, this dysfunctional state often shows itself first in the psychiatrist by a tendency to be absent more frequently; the psychiatrist seems to take more and more vacations and also misses more and more days of work for various minor ailments. In the cases I have seen, this behavior has been a manifestation not — as it is often rationalized to be — of the aging process and flagging energies, but of a gradually developing depression and despair. In some cases, this despair is denied through growing

399

megalomanic paternalism towards patients, or sometimes a refusal to listen to patients at all except to regulate drug doses in progressively shorter “treatment” sessions. This does not necessarily result in the loss of patients because there are a number of patients who need a figure they can idealize as a god-like and unapproachable physician who has all the answers, which gives them temporary relief.

My general impression is that the higher income that accrues to the practitioner of reductionistic biological psychiatry often at least temporarily compensates for any fleeting suspicions of inauthenticity. Therefore, my final question is an ethical one: Should the leaders of American psychiatry embrace the biological paradigm that will make certification easier and reward us with the material things of this world, or should psychiatry press forward as a revolutionary and humanizing force calling attention to inequities, racism, sexism, and all the ills of which society is capable, at the risk of political opprobrium, financial loss, and, even in some Marxist countries, brutal repression? Should the leaders of American psychiatry commit our profession to an amelioration of those psychological and sociological factors that enter into the very fabric of society, or should they constrain our discipline so that it wears the trappings of internal medicine and thus gains respectability in a culture that values “fast, fast, fast relief” — where drugs are used for everything, to the ecstatic joy of the large drug corporations that saturate our advertising media and even our professional journals and meetings with their simplistic sales messages.

The American Psychiatric Association recently assessed all its members for the construction of a new building. Parkinson (1957) in one of his famous laws writes: “The perfection of a planned layout is achieved only by institutions on the point of collapse…. During a period of exciting discovery or progress there is no time to plan the perfect headquarters. The time for that comes when all the important work has been done” (pp. 60-61).2 I sincerely hope this will not be true for American psychiatry, and that we will remember

2I am indebted to Dr. Daniel Schiff for this quotation.400

the lesson from the history of psychiatry as taught by Zilboorg (1941):

The whole course of the history of medical psychology is punctuated by the medical man's struggle to rise above the prejudices of all ages in order to identify himself with the psychological realities of his patients. Every time such an identification was achieved the medical man became a psychiatrist. The history of psychiatry is essentially the history of humanism. Every time humanism has diminished or degenerated into mere philanthropic sentimentality, psychiatry has entered a new ebb. Every time the spirit of humanism has arisen, a new contribution to psychiatry has been made [pp. 524-525].

As Karl Jaspers said, the doctor is indeed the patient's fate.

This essay on various aspects of mirroring is written with the hope that it might correct some common misconceptions. My focus is on the technical considerations of mirroring in the clinical psychoanalytic situation. In the almost two decades since Kohut (1968) first described the mirror transference as the patient's insistent demands on the analyst for the latter's confirming presence, this term has become familiar to many psychoanalysts. However, along with many other psychoanalytic terms, mirroring, mirror transference, and selfobject are defined more by common, agreed-upon usage than by reference to a generally accepted theoretical framework. I would define selfobjects as a special class of objects—or of symbols or ideas representing objects—that perform the specific functions of providing a self-evoking and self-sustaining experience to the potential and to the emerged self. Strictly speaking, therefore, selfobjects are neither self nor object; they are the subjective aspect of a function performed by a relationship. As such, the selfobject relationship refers to an intrapsychic experience and does not describe the interpersonal relationship between the self and other objects. It denotes the experience of imagos that are needed for the sustenance of the self.

Henry Krystal  

As psychoanalysts we are most comfortable dealing with the kind of material we derive from our clinical practice: fantasies, conflicts, resistances, defenses, couched in familiar terms of classical formulations. However, our complacency is disturbed by patients who do not fit comfortably into these conceptions. Such difficulties have developed for me in trying to deal with a very large population of survivors of the Nazi Holocaust. Repeatedly, in my early publications, I despaired over the possibility of understanding the phenomena of the post-traumatic residues and the process of traumatization in terms of classical conceptions (Krystal, 1968, 1971).

Finding that I could not explain all the phenomena observed in survivors, particularly the concentration camp inmates, I proceeded to describe the findings, hoping that they would eventually add up to material by which the process of traumatization and recovery could be understood in greater depth and accuracy. I was finally able to formulate a concept of massive traumatization (1978a) that corresponded to what I had learned from my patients. In these formulations I tried to understand the common basis of their experience and to account for the occurrence of certain symptoms not previously explainable. Such post-traumatic pictures included alexithymia, inhibitions in the capacity for self-caring, anhedonia, continuation of extreme hypervigilance, depressive and masochistic patterns, as well as characteristic personality patterns.

Dr. Krystal is Professor of Psychiatry, Michigan State University, East Lansing, Michigan.

It is possible to live in a twilight between knowing and not knowing.

The issues of knowing and not knowing permeate the Holocaust on numerous levels. On the level of political decision making, let there be no doubt that the degree of knowing of available information had a far-reaching impact on the course of historical events during World War II (Laqueur, 1980). On the level of personal experience to which we as clinicians have access, the conflict around knowing the Holocaust is ubiquitous. There is the survivor's claim to privileged knowledge by virtue of his experience—“I know the truth about people,” “I know something about human nature that others don't”—as well as the question that haunts the survivor, “How could the world countenance the Holocaust by pretending not to know?” (Langer, 1982). There is the perpetrator's disclaimer, “I didn't know,” and subsequent generations' question to victims, “Why didn't you know?” There is our admiring query of the few resisters to evil, “How did you know (how to act)?” and the question posed now, as we contemplate future genocides

Knowing the Holocaust

Robert Prince PHD

Robert Prince

48 Beverly Road
Great Neck, New York 11021

Robert Prince  

I am roughly the same age now that my father was when he had his first child. The difference between us is that the Holocaust ripped him away from his family and forced him into a slave labor battalion, whereas I remain free to support my family in my chosen profession as a psychologist.

I have a desire to pass on to my infant son knowledge about the Holocaust in general and of his grandfather's experience of survivorhood in particular. Because this impulse in me is spontaneous, without reflection or conscious decision — a psychological given — I find it important to understand what I mean by it: just what it is I want to pass on, and why it seems to be a psychological imperative to do so.

In this desire to tell my son about the Holocaust, I share what seems to be a common desire to children of survivors. Of particular note is that in a broad and exhaustive study of children of survivors (Prince, 1985a), this desire was one of the few discrete traits held in common among children of survivors. Whereas dramatic differences exist in conscious identification or in self-attribution of importance to having been children of survivors, in personality styles, in preferred modes of interpersonal relationship, in relationships to parents, in Jewish identification, in attitudes, ideas, and beliefs in general and about the Holocaust in particular, children of survivors universally want to pass on knowledge of the Holocaust.

Models and values that are deeply internalized create the strength to resist every alien system which denies those values. This does not mean that these models and values could be put into action in their pure form at Auschwitz. Translated into the language of everyday camp conditions, they defined the field of each individual's battle, on which he sustained defeats as well as victories.

When at the end of the second world war the gates of the concentration camps opened, the people who walked out of them looked like a strange and frightening horde even to those Europeans who by that time had seen all that combat, bombings, and starvation could do to the human body and mind. Lacan's Mirror Stage

John Muller PHD

John Muller

Stockbridge, Massachusetts 01262

John Muller  

Mirror phenomena are increasingly receiving more consideration, but with the increased attention has come a diffusion of meaning. Dervin (1980) sees mirroring as perhaps “a quite natural phenomenon that contributes to both self and object representations” (p. 138). On the other hand, Goldberg (1984) treats the double as a mirror phenomenon and views the double as a second self but, at the same time, also a counter-self and a “mirror” of unacknowledged, even unattainable aspects of oneself. Thus, what is mirrored can include what is visible at the surface as well as what is not visible, disavowed, and even impossible. (In this usage, the mirror becomes not a reflector but a kind of magical window). While Goldberg rightly stresses how mirror phenomena cast doubt on the notion (and experience) of the self's unity and identity, Pines (1984) wants to show the mirror conveying identity, whereas, in contrast, the mirroring responses of others reflect differences. Pines emphasizes that the mother's selective responses to the child's behaviors reinforce certain behaviors and thereby promote an identity; “basically the same invariant personal theme of identity has been laid down in a mirroring relationship to mother” (p. 32). But under the category of the mirroring response, Pines includes a wide variety of responses and in the process seems to equate feedback and responsiveness of any sort with a mirroring response.

Mirrors and Mirroring: Developmental Experiences

Joseph Lichtenberg MD

Joseph Lichtenberg

1616 Eighteenth St., N. W.
Washington, D. C. 20009

Joseph Lichtenberg  

Polished Metal or Stone has been employed for its reflective property for at least 5,000 years. Despite the familiarity of a reflecting surface, the word we use for it, mirror, is derived from mirari “to wonder.” Thus, like the sun, moon, and stars, like birth and death, a reflecting surface, its ubiquity notwithstanding, elicited in man a sense of wonder, puzzlement, and continuous fascination. The roots of the word appear also in miracle and mirage — suggesting the fantastic and the illusory. Like its synonym, reflecting, mirroring has acquired both a physical and a psychological meaning. But while physical reflecting is limited in complexity to the laws of optics, psychic reflecting is extremely rich and varied, reflection being central to human mentation. Similarly, while physical mirroring can bring back only the rays that are put into it, the mirroring of a mother to her child, of an analyst to an analysand, of a friend to a friend, conveys back not only recognition but emotional resonance — a response that establishes the humanity of the two partners in the exchange. Moreover, at any moment the mirroring mother, analyst, or friend may turn into an initiator, seeking in turn a response of emotional attunement. My point is this: drawing analogies from the physical mirror to psychic mirroring is rich in its metaphoric connotations but subject to misleading blurring of distinctions. In this paper I attempt to describe the infant's reaction to the physical mirror as a discrete entity.

Dr. Lichtenberg is on the faculty of the Washington Psychoanalytic Institute.

I am concerned in this paper with the capacity of children of Holocaust survivors to tolerate affects and the construction, in collaboration with a therapist, of a narrative account of data from the remembered, fantasized, and hitherto unexplored past. The experimental and observational study of mirroring in children contributes to understanding the developmental lines of self as subject, self as object, and self with object. To this widely recognized schema can be added the unusual tangential contribution of Lacan and the French school: self as other.

Categorization artifically separates the growth of the whole person into components, the person in relation to others. Milton Jucovy  

The issue of knowing and not knowing is at the very core of our psychoanalytic work as we attempt to help our patients resolve their unconscious conflicts. This process may be described in terms of Freud's topographic model of the mind as trying to render conscious what has been unconscious, or formulated on the basis of his later structural theory as attempting to alter forces in the patient's psychic structure so that pathological defenses are undermined and replaced by healthier ego activities. During these efforts, we are continually working with secrets, the revelation of which we trust will bring about dynamic, structural, and economic changes that are consistent with the display of greater adaptational capacities. Although encounters with secrets are ubiquitous in psychoanalytic work, it is also true that their presence and impact are more apparent in members of certain groups. The purpose of this contribution is to report some of the observations yielded by a study of survivors of the Holocaust and their children, with particular emphasis on communication between the generations. We have learned that certain features of a child's development may be influenced by parental withholding of information and that even well-intentioned revelations of parental experiences may be shrouded in uncertainty, distortion, or mystery.

Joseph Lichtenberg  

Anew baby coming into a family, a three-month-old flashing a smile, a six-month-old crawling, and a one-year-old looking to mother for guidance are such manifestly lively presences that it seems puzzling that psychoanalysis, approaching its centenary, is still actively seeking to discover the essential nature of infancy — or at least remains embroiled in controversies about the babyhood its retrospective focus has reconstructed.

In Psychoanalysis and Infant Research I sought to illuminate many of the controversies by presenting alternative concepts of the nature of infantile life gleaned from the works of experimental and observational researchers, trying always to present in summary form the data on which the alternative view is based. Now I, as well as you, the reader of the commentaries presented here, have an opportunity to reconfront many of these controversies as they are stated with vigor and clarity by the essayists: Have I failed to go far enough in advocating the abandonment of outmoded inaccurate theories (Demos)? Have I gone too far in my critique of drive theory (Dowling)? Have I taken too much of a phenomenologist position and understated the intrapsychic organization (Gedo)? Have I failed to utilize sufficiently the valuable direct observations of Mahler on separation individuation while overstating the influence of cognitive processes (Bergman and Pollens)?

W. Meissner  

Introduction

The recent history of psychoanalysis has been characterized by a chaotic jumble of theories, each contending for its place in the sun and each striving to establish hegemony over rival theories. What occasioned this rivalrous squabbling and contentiousness in a field where the psychology of Sigmund Freud reigned for so many years unchallenged and unquestioned? Had the father of the psychoanalytic primal horde finally been unseated and cast to the dust? Were the quarrelsome sons at each other's throats in an attempt to establish a new hegemony, a new psychoanalytic vision of man that would vanquish the views of the founding father and establish a reign of deeper and more fulsome psychoanalytic understanding?

For many years, Freud's own theories, particularly the overriding structural hypothesis and its commitment to a corresponding metapsychology, dominated the field. But scientific theories, regardless of whose genius has created them, are never adequate; they are always to some degree and in some respect false. Reality, and particularly the reality of human nature, can never be captured in a theory.

There can be no doubt that all knowledge begins with experience … Though all our knowledge begins with experience it does not follow that it all arises out of experience …

During the first five years of Psychoanalytic Inquiry's publication, a variety of topics have been explored ranging from Values and Neutrality and Reconstruction in Psychoanalysis to Psychoanalytic Models and new developments in Infant Research. In the papers devoted to each topic, we have been impressed that the issues discussed frequently are traced to attempts to reconcile the dialectic in psychoanalysis between science and humanism. Questions have been repeatedly asked concerning the proper balance between objectivism and subjectivism, meaning and causality, psychology and metapsychology, phenomenology and abstraction.

We believe further developments in psychoanalytic understanding are contingent on a clarification of the place of psychoanalysis within the realm of science. The claim of psychoanalysis for a place within science has been questioned because the methodology and data of psychoanalysis are based on human interaction and subjective experience. Psychoanalysis can answer that it encompasses both a scientifically based theory of mental functioning and the larger problems of human existence. What makes this so vital an area for exploration is that the issues on both sides of the dialectic between science and humanism are constantly changing, and these changes must be reflected in psychoanalysis. Freud's contribution evolved from the 19th and early 20th century's view of science, strongly influenced by positive objectivism with emphasis on the separation of objectivism and subjectivism.

Epilogue

Nanette Auerhahn Issue Editor and Dori Laub Issue Editor

Dori Laub

Dori Laub  

In thinking about the foregoing articles, we now ask: How is the Holocaust known? The answer appears to be: in fragments. That is, trauma is both registered and manifested in fragments.

Regarding trauma's manner of registration: Trauma bombards and fragments the mind, which can neither symbolize nor integrate the experience.

Regarding trauma's manner of manifestation: Trauma is remembered and reappears in fragments. What the researcher sees is neither universal themes nor syndromes but particular startling phenomena, which in a given individual have a unique stamp. That is, trauma does not appear as a major organizer of personality alone, but in addition shows itself in discrete ways, whether these be symptoms, daydreams, poems, fantasies, or characteristic traits. It permeates life in fragments, in circumscribed phenomena that are usually overlooked by those searching for trends and generalizations.

If the survivor is to know the Holocaust, he must reassemble his fragmentary perceptions. Only then can he mourn, for “one cannot grieve what one does not know” (Reeves, 1973, p. 26).

Likewise, if researchers are to know the Holocaust, they must attend to the details wherein the threads of trauma appear. We must take the details and form a narrative from them, one interwoven with personality factors, in order to understand trauma's impact and arrive at something more central and cohesive than the fragments but not a substitute for them. Too often researchers have lumped survivors together into groups (e.g., Danieli, 1979) and have done the equivalent of dream translation rather than dream interpretation, deriving an overriding theory that has superseded and replaced the text, the details.
